newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS-EMU optimists see divergence drying up.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS-EMU optimists see divergence drying up.

text.p: European bond markets will look to this weekend's meeting of European finance ministers for signals that there is room to unwind divergence trades, economists said on Friday.
"There was a big convergence play in 1996, but so far in 1997 we have had divergence," said Ken Wattret, international economist at Paribas Capital Markets in London.
"Yet there is no longer the atmosphere of panic which was evident in March," he added.
European finance ministers meet informally on Saturday.

The official agenda for the session in the Dutch town of Noordwijk concentrates on negotiations to settle any outstanding issues in the Stability and Growth Pact, a framework to ensure fiscal discipline under European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
"The meeting will look at who will benefit from the fines, but that is not likely to move the market," said Wattret.
More important for the bond markets, economists said, was EMU-friendly German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's announcement on Thursday that he planned to stand for re-election in 1998.
"It is a fairly strong signal that the political will is there for EMU to go ahead on time," said Philip Tyson, senior international economist at HSBC Midland in London.
"We expect to hear some fairly EMU-positive noises from the meeting."
The threat of a delay to EMU, the third stage of which is scheduled to take place in January 1999, has spooked European bond markets in the past few weeks.
The BTP/Bund spread widened from around 180 basis points in early January to as high as 218 basis points in mid-March. At the beginning of 1996, the spread was around 475 basis points.
But signs of commitment to a firm EMU timetable from this weekend's meeting will benefit Italy less than other peripheral European bond markets, economists said.
"EMU will push ahead on time, and Spain and Portugal will be in there with the core group, but Italy will not make it," Tyson predicted.
"You should be buying Spain versus Italy," he added.
Paribas' Wattret also sees Spain able to join EMU in 1999.
"The economy is continuing to grow and inflation has fallen sharply. The chances of Spain entering on time are something better than 50:50."
Huw Roberts, European bond strategist at NatWest Markets in London, expects the BTP/Bund spread to trade in a 200-250 basis point range over the next few months.

The shorter-term outlook for Italy is more promising, Roberts said. The lira strengthened beyond its Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) central parity level of 990 lira to the mark earlier on Friday. It was at 991.30 per mark at 1138 GMT.
"But if we have a strong payrolls figure, the dollar will be undermined and that does not bode well for BTPs or bonos," he added.

U.S. March employment data are due at 1330 GMT on Friday and are forecast to show a rise in non-farm payrolls of 196,000. A strong number would increase speculation of tighter U.S. credit, normally a dollar positive but potentially a negative if it sparked widespread U.S. asset declines, analysts said.
Markets will also be affected by indications from the weekend meeting as to which countries hold the upper hand in the EMU debate.
"There will be wrangling between the periphery and the core over budget deficits, as to whether a strong performance in 1997 will allow EMU membership," said Wattret.
Bond markets will pounce on any sign of discord behind the scenes, away from the expected positive official stance on the EMU timetable, economists said.
